replies: I'll mock you. First question: "Tell me about yourself and why this role." Answer in one to three minutes as you would in the interview; I'll score it for structure, evidence and specificity, give one concrete improvement, then ask the next question. Ready?

Score: 2/10.

Why: Structure barely present (no clear S-T-A-R), zero evidence of outcome or impact, light on specifics (no timeframe, tools, constraints, your exact role).

One concrete improvement (use STAR + a metric + tool):
- Situation: one line naming the company/team and why the model was needed.
- Task: one sentence: your responsibility and the deadline.
- Action: two sentences: the model scope (three‑statement), main drivers you built (e.g. units, price, churn), the tool (Excel/Sheets) and a key assumption you stress‑tested.
- Result: one sentence with a number or concrete outcome (cost/time saved, forecast accuracy, a decision enabled).
Example rewrite you can adapt (keep or replace brackets):
"Situation: at [Company] the finance team needed a quarterly forecast after a product launch because revenue was volatile. Task: I was asked to deliver a three‑statement forecast in three days to inform the Q3 spend decision. Action: I built a three‑statement model in [your skill] linking revenue drivers (units, price, adoption rate) to COGS and working capital, stress‑tested three scenarios and benchmarked margins against three public comps. Result: my model showed a [number] downside to EBITDA in the base case, which led leadership to delay a hire and cut discretionary spend by 8%, preserving runway; the CFO used my numbers in guidance."
One concrete fix to apply now: add a measurable result (even if approximate and stated as such: "identified a 12% downside") and the tool you used.

Next question (mock continues): Tell me about a time you worked with a team under a deadline. Answer in one to three minutes as you would in the interview; I'll score it the same way and give one improvement. Is that the next question you want?

Honest score: 2/10.

Why, plainly:
- Structure (1/3): It's a single tactical sentence, not a STAR. No Situation or clear Task described.
- Evidence (0/4): No project, timeline, your specific role, tools, or concrete inputs shown.
- Specificity (1/3): Mentions "revenue drivers" and "comps" but doesn't name which drivers, which comps, or how you'd test them.

What it sounds like to an interviewer: a checklist item — you know the right components but didn't show you executed them or drove a decision. That invites follow-ups like "Which drivers?" "Give me an example" or "What was the impact?" where you'll struggle without details.
One concrete improvement right now (do this and you'll move to 6–7/10):
- Turn it into a 30–45 second STAR: name the company or context and the problem, state your role and deadline, list the key drivers you modeled (pick 2–3: e.g., MAU, ARPU, conversion), name the tool (Excel/Sheets/Modeling language), say one analytic step (scenario or sensitivity on a driver), and finish with a quantified result or decision your model changed (if you don't have an exact number, give a conservative estimate and label it "~").
Example you can say aloud: "At [Company], finance needed a one-week forecast after a product launch. I owned a three‑statement model in Excel linking MAU and ARPU to revenue, built COGS and working-capital schedules, ran three scenarios and a sensitivity on MAU ±20%. The model showed a ~12% downside to EBITDA in the base case, which led leadership to delay hiring and cut discretionary spend, preserving runway." Replace brackets with your facts.

Want me to quiz you next with the team-deadline question I proposed, or do you want to rewrite this answer now and I'll rescore it?

replies:
Good — I’ll prep you for final rounds at Lincoln International with a focused, practical plan and immediate mock questions you can practice now.
What I’ll give you now
- Short interview brief: what Lincoln will test in final rounds and the single most important impression to leave.
- 8-step, timed prep plan you can run in the next 4 hours.
- Four STAR story templates to fill with your facts (teamwork, failure, problem solving, senior interaction).
- Technical refresh checklist (valuation, LBO, DCF, working capital, common accounting adjustments).
- Six mock final-round questions we can practice now; when you answer I’ll score structure, evidence and specificity and give one concrete fix, then ask the next.
Interview brief (what they test and the one impression to leave)
- What they test: technical accuracy and speed on valuation and transaction math; clear frameworks on case / modeling questions; deal judgment (value drivers, synergies, risks); fit for long hours and client-facing work (coachability, concise explanations); attention to detail and professional communication.
- One impression to leave: you are technically fluent and calm under pressure — you show rapid, structured thinking (framework first, then math) and you connect every technical point to deal impact.
8-step timed prep plan (do these in order; total ~3–4 hours)
1) 30–45 min — Core technical review: one-page cheat sheet covering enterprise vs equity value, WACC inputs, FCFF formula, terminal value methods, LBO sources & uses, basic IRR vs equity multiple relationship.
2) 30 min — Walk one deal end-to-end: pick a deal you know (or a recent Lincoln deal you can cite). In 3–4 bullets: business, strategic rationale, valuation approach, your contribution or what you’d change.
3) 25–40 min — Quick calculations drill: 3 short exercises (implied EV/EBITDA from numbers; 3-year FCFF with simple assumptions; IRR for a 3-year hold). Time yourself per problem (15–20 min each).
4) 45–60 min — Mock case: one timed case where you speak through approach, assumptions, and a simple calculation; I’ll score structure and gaps.
5) 20–30 min — Behavioral stories: write four STAR answers, each 60–90 seconds — teamwork, failure, problem-solve, senior interaction. Use metrics.
6) 10–15 min — Why Lincoln: draft 2–3 reasons tied to the firm’s deal focus or a recent deal and one personal fit point (training, client exposure, culture).
7) 10–15 min — Questions you’ll ask them: prepare 6 sharp questions about deal pipeline, typical team structure on a mandate, recent challenge on a deal, training, performance feedback, and next steps.
8) 5 min — Logistics and mental checklist: camera/audio, printed resume, calculator, one-page notes, breathe, structure-first, narrate assumptions.
Technical refresh checklist (be fluent in these)
- Enterprise vs equity value adjustments: net debt, minority interest, preferred, leases (IFRS/US GAAP treatment).
- WACC: cost of equity (beta, market premium), cost of debt (pre-tax vs after-tax), target capital structure, tax rate.
- DCF: FCFF formula, explicit forecast to free cash flow, terminal value (perpetuity growth and exit multiple), sensitivity table basics.
- LBO basics: sources & uses, debt tranches, amortization vs bullet, how leverage and multiple changes drive IRR and equity multiple.
- Valuation cross-checks: when comps vs precedent transactions vs DCF dominate and why they produce different answers.
- Working capital mechanics: NWC as % of revenue vs absolute change; capex vs depreciation effects on free cash flow.

STAR templates (fill with your facts)
- Teamwork: Situation, your role, specific actions to coordinate or resolve, measurable outcome (time saved, closed milestones, improved metric).
- Failure/mistake: Brief situation, what you owned, what you changed (process), and the positive result or lesson.
- Problem solving/insight: Situation, the analysis you ran or insight you found, how it changed the recommendation, measurable impact.
- Senior/client interaction: Situation, the pushback or ask, how you presented your case and adjusted, and the delivered result.
Six mock final-round questions (pick one to start; I’ll time you if you want)
1) Walk me through a DCF from revenue to equity value. Where do you spend the most judgment?
2) Here’s a short case: estimate implied EV/EBITDA given revenue, margin and a comparable multiple; say how you’d sanity-check it.
3) Tell me about a deal you worked on (or would pitch): what was the biggest value driver and what did you do about it?
4) Why Lincoln International and why this team?
5) Describe a time you disagreed with a teammate or senior. What did you say and what happened?
6) If you had to improve a company’s free cash flow in 12 months, what three levers would you prioritize and why?
How I’ll score your answers in the mock
- I score on three things: structure (clear framework first), evidence (concrete actions, numbers), specificity (one measurable result or exact assumption). After each answer I give one concrete improvement and then the next question.

Next step now
- Tell me which mock question to start with (or say “start with Q1 timed”). If you want me to draft your 60–90 second “deal pitch” and 2–3 Lincoln-specific reasons instead, say that and I’ll draft them (I’ll need either the deal name or permission to pick a recent Lincoln deal).

When you give me the posting (link or role+city), I will prepare an application card for your approval. Here is exactly what I will fill in and send to the card for you to review, field by field — what I will include, what I will ask you to confirm, and what stays blank until you type it:

- Full name — from the resume/contact you saved.

- Employer name (exact).

- Job location or remote tag (exact).
- Link to posting (exact).
- Job description and required skills (the text).
- Pay as listed (or “not listed”).
- Application method required (company form, email, external board).
- Any screening questions called out in the posting.
What I will prepare for the application card fields you must review and edit
- Resume to attach — I will attach the resume chosen; you may swap it.
- Cover note / short message — a 1–3 paragraph tailored note I draft for this posting. I will mark any bracketed items you must fill (e.g., availability, manager name) and keep it under ~300 words. You review and edit it on the card.
- Answers to posting screening questions — I will draft concise answers from your confirmed facts where possible; blank where missing and flagged for you to fill.
- Work history fields the employer asks for (dates, titles) — pre-filled from your confirmed facts where possible; I will flag any gaps or mismatches for you to correct.
- Salary expectation / current compensation — left blank unless you ask me to populate; I will note the posting pay/market numbers if given.
- References — left blank; I will put a reminder to add them if the posting asks.
- Portfolio / code links — I will include any links you confirmed on file; otherwise blank.
- Attachments (cover letter, certificates, transcripts) — I will attach those you have confirmed; otherwise noted as optional.
What I will NOT fill or send without your explicit edit/approval
- Any personal statement you haven’t confirmed.
- Any reference contact details.
- Any answers that require a one-time code, CAPTCHA or employer-specific verification.
- Any changes to your saved resume contact info unless you edit it on the card.
What the card will show you before anything is sent (exact approval steps)
1. Posting header: company, title, location, pay (if listed), link.
2. My tailored cover note draft (with [brackets] where I need you).
3. Resume file attached (name and 7‑day link).
4. Each screening question with my drafted answer and an edit button.
5. Any extra attachments I plan to add and an option to remove.
6. A final checklist of required fields still blank (phone, salary, references, work authorization, etc.).
7. Two action buttons: “Approve and queue” (puts it in your apply queue for the extension to pick up) and “Edit” (lets you change any field).
One more thing I will show separately if the posting routes applications by email or an external board
- Exact subject line I will use for the employer email (drafted for you).
- The exact recipient email or external link and any instructions I saw on the posting (e.g., “send portfolio link in body”).
- The short email body I will paste into the employer’s form or email client (under 120 words).

What I will record on your account when you approve the card
- The exact resume and cover note version used.
- The date/time you approved it.
Next step: paste the job link or tell me the role + city you mean by “the first one” and I will read the posting and prepare that card exactly as above. Is that the posting you mean?
